name: Sara Alvarez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for having me, Sara. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no links to AI companies, employers, unions or political parties, and we don't sell anything. Everything you say is confidential. Could you tell me about a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at Whitaker's, the sock mill on Bridge Street, which has been in the same family for three generations. I mind six circular knitting machines, the ones that knit the sock as a tube, so I'm threading yarn, swapping cones when they run low, catching dropped stitches and pulling off any socks with holes before they go to the toe-closing room. Two years now, and I still can't hear when a needle's about to break the way the older ladies can. Mrs Doyle can tell from across the floor, and I'm still learning to listen.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What brought you to the mill?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I stayed home with Lucia and Mateo until Mateo started school properly, which is how we were brought up. Then Luis's overtime on the council roads crew was cut, and we needed a second wage for the mortgage. My mother worked at a mill too, so it felt right. I like that it's honest work, you can hold what you made at the end of the day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, people got carried away. I'm not on the internet much, so I'd say it after church or to my sister on the phone. Most of the fuss comes from people who've never made anything with their hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I keep learning my machines and the mill keeps going. That's all I want. Mr Whitaker isn't one for spending money on gadgets anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on as we are. Keep the bit we've saved, about two months, and put a little more by when Luis gets overtime. Maybe ask Mrs Doyle to teach me the needle changes properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Thankful, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you use any of these AI tools yourself, or does anyone at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I don't, and I don't want to. Lucia uses something for school, and I check what she's looking at. I'd rather the children learned to think for themselves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want for the mill in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: More orders, so Mr Whitaker can take on a couple of the young ones from the estate as apprentices. That's how it should work, the old teaching the young.

S0.say: People got carried away, and most of the fuss came from people who've never made anything with their hands. She'd say it after church or to her sister on the phone.
S0.think: She keeps learning her machines and the mill keeps going, which is all she wants. The mill owner isn't one for spending money on gadgets anyway.
S0.do: Carries on as normal and keeps the two months of savings, adding a little when her husband gets overtime. Asks the experienced knitter to teach her needle changes properly.
S0.quote: Most of the fuss comes from people who've never made anything with their hands.
S0.fieldNote: Sara values work you can hold and learning passed from older workers to younger ones. She doesn't use AI and doesn't want her children relying on it. A flat future matches both her hopes and her trust in her cautious employer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say businesses have to stay competitive, that's just how it is. But people should get the chance to work, and families shouldn't be thrown on the scrap heap. I'd say we need more apprenticeships, not handouts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the big sock factories abroad would get the robots first and undercut us. Then Mr Whitaker would have to choose between new machines and closing. Either way, the newest one goes first, and that's me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put a bit more aside, maybe thirty a week, and stop the little extras. I'd work harder to learn from Mrs Doyle so I'm worth keeping. I wouldn't do computer courses, I'd stick to what I know and pray on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not frightened yet, but it's there in the back of my mind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Mr Whitaker doesn't spend on gadgets. Do you think that protects you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For a while. He's careful, and the family won't want to borrow. But if the big firms go cheap, he'll have no choice, and I wouldn't blame him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the mill did change, what would you be willing to do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anything that's hands-on. Moving to the toe-closing room, or packing. I'd rather do a lesser job than sit at a screen.

S1.say: Businesses have to stay competitive, but people should get the chance to work and families shouldn't be thrown on the scrap heap. She'd call for more apprenticeships, not handouts.
S1.think: Big factories abroad would automate first and undercut the mill, forcing the owner to choose between new machines and closing. Either way, the newest worker goes first, and that's her.
S1.do: Puts about thirty a week aside and cuts small extras. Works harder to learn from the experienced knitter so she's worth keeping, avoiding computer courses.
S1.feel: Uneasy, not frightened yet but with worry in the back of her mind.
S1.quote: I'd rather do a lesser job than sit at a screen.
S1.fieldNote: Sara blames competition from big foreign firms rather than her employer, whom she'd forgive. Her trust in the mill's cautious owners keeps her worry at a low level for now. She'd take a lower job rather than learn screen-based work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is wrong and it's going too fast. Families matter more than profits. I'd say we need to look after our own, through church and family, because the government won't get it right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I think the mill would close, or bring in machines that don't need me. I'm 43 with no qualifications and I don't use computers. I don't know what I'd do, and that keeps me up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd stop everything we don't need. I'd ask at church about help and lean on my brother, who's got a building firm, for any work. And I'd look for cleaning or care jobs, anything with my hands, while they lasted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened. Like walking in fog.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years. What would you do in the first week?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pray, honestly, and then sit down with Luis and go through every bill. Ring the bank before we missed anything. And tell the children nothing's changing at home, whatever happens outside.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Luis works for the council. Does that feel safer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, for a while. Roads still need fixing. But if robots can do it all, the council would buy them too, to save money. So maybe a year more than me.

S2.say: It's wrong and it's going too fast, because families matter more than profits. She'd say people need to look after their own through church and family, since the government won't get it right.
S2.think: The mill would close or bring in machines that don't need her, and at 43 with no qualifications and no computer skills she doesn't know what she'd do. It keeps her up at night.
S2.do: Cuts everything the family doesn't need and rings the bank before any payment is missed. Asks her church and her brother's building firm for help and looks for cleaning or care work.
S2.quote: Tell the children nothing's changing at home, whatever happens outside.
S2.fieldNote: Her response is anchored in faith and family rather than the state, consistent with her views. Her husband's council job gives only a slight buffer in her eyes. She wants to shield her children from the upheaval, even if it isn't fully true.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time, so families should prepare and help each other. Businesses should train people up, not just throw them out. I'd say it plainly to anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years means I could get more savings in and get the children further through school. But it ends the same, with me out of the mill. I'd just be a bit more ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save harder, forty or fifty a week, and pay extra off the mortgage. I'd ask my brother about learning some practical skills at his building firm, like tiling or decorating. And I'd keep my head down at the mill as long as it lasted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with time to pray on it and plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years. Would that change anything about what you'd learn?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, if it's hands-on. Tiling, painting, sewing alterations. Not computers, I'm too old for that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want for Lucia and Mateo in that time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A trade, for both of them. Something they can do with their hands, with a good master to teach them. Lucia wants to be a nurse, and that's good, people will always want a person when they're ill.

S3.say: There's time, so families should prepare and help each other, and businesses should train people up rather than throw them out. She'd say it plainly to anyone.
S3.think: Five years means more savings and her children further through school, but it still ends with her out of the mill. She'd just be a bit more ready.
S3.do: Saves forty or fifty a week and pays extra off the mortgage. Asks her brother about learning tiling or decorating at his building firm, and keeps her head down at the mill as long as it lasts.
S3.feel: Anxious, but with time to pray on it and plan.
S3.quote: Not computers, I'm too old for that.
S3.fieldNote: With more time, Sara becomes open to learning a hands-on trade through her family network, though not anything digital. She wants trades for her children too and is pleased her daughter wants nursing. Her faith gives her a sense of steadiness rather than solving anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got time to get it right, so let's do it the proper way, with apprenticeships and families looking after each other. No handouts, but real work. I'd say that at church and to anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is a long time. Lucia would be 23, Mateo 20, both working, I hope. I'd be 53 and still with a mortgage, but I'd have time to learn something with my hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep working at the mill, keep saving, and in a few years go to my brother's firm to learn a trade properly. Make sure the children get into trades or nursing. I'd wait to see what Mr Whitaker does before making any big moves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious still, but more settled. It's in God's hands and I've got time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, what's the first thing you'd do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep saving, a bit more each month, and start talking to my brother about tiling. Get Mateo thinking about an apprenticeship.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you think the ten years would let the mill find a way through?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. People pay more for socks made by a family firm, with a person's name on the label. Mr Whitaker might find his little corner. I'd want to be part of that.

S4.say: There's time to get it right the proper way, with apprenticeships and families looking after each other. She'd say no handouts but real work, at church and to anyone.
S4.think: Ten years is long enough for both children to be working and for her to learn something with her hands. She'd still be 53 with a mortgage.
S4.do: Keeps working and saving, and in a few years learns tiling at her brother's firm. Steers her children into trades or nursing and waits to see what the mill owner does before making big moves.
S4.feel: Still anxious but more settled, trusting God and the time she has.
S4.quote: People pay more for socks made by a family firm, with a person's name on the label.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade, Sara hopes the mill might survive in a niche where human-made goods are valued. Her plans run through family: her brother's firm and her children's trades. She remains anxious because her own options still feel narrow.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, without a doubt, because there's no time to learn anything or save anything. What would help is apprenticeships for grown-ups like me, paid, with a real person teaching. Not a website, a person.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about church. When things go wrong, that's where people go round here, not the job centre. If all of this happens, it'll be the church halls feeding people, mark my words.

headlineQuote: If all of this happens, it'll be the church halls feeding people, mark my words.
portrait: Sara Alvarez, 43, minds six sock-knitting machines at a three-generation family mill, two years in after staying home with her children, and still learning to hear a needle about to break. She never uses AI, wants her children to think for themselves, and favours apprenticeships and family over handouts. She trusts her careful employer and blames big foreign firms, so steady change leaves her only uneasy, but fast AGI frightens her and sends her to church and her brother. With more time she'd learn a hands-on trade and hopes a family-made label might keep the mill alive.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because there would be no time to learn anything new or save anything.
whatWouldHelp: Paid apprenticeships for adults like her, taught by a real person rather than a website.
